terminal.description: A shell in your workspace: node run.mjs <file> runs every statement in that file on a fresh copy of the practice's database, prints each query plan you ask for, and saves nothing.

tasks.title: Index the visits by date
tasks.description:
Winnie looks up the visits of one day many times a day, and today SQLite reads every visit to find them.

In `queries/1-visit-dates.sql`, above the plan that is already there, write a `CREATE INDEX` so that a search on `visits` by `visit_date` uses it: for one date, and for a range of dates.

Check runs only your `CREATE INDEX` and `DROP INDEX` statements, on its own fresh copy of the database. Then it asks SQLite for the plan of two searches of its own, one for a single date and one for a range, and looks for your index in each plan.
nextSteps: Run the file as it is and read the plan: what does `SCAN visits` mean?
Write a `CREATE INDEX` with a name of your own, on the table and the column the search looks up.
Run the file again and read the plan: it should name your index.
hints: Read the lesson's parts "Reading a plan" and "Making an index". Which column does Winnie's search look up?
An index is on one table, and on the columns a search compares. After `ON` come the table and, in brackets, the column.
The statement has the shape `CREATE INDEX visits_by_date ON visits (...);`.

tasks.title: Index the animals by owner
tasks.description:
Finding an owner's animals reads every row of `animals`, whether the search is on its own or a join from `owners`.

In `queries/2-animals-by-owner.sql`, write a `CREATE INDEX` on `animals` that both use, and an `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` of your own to read the plan before and after.

Check runs only your `CREATE INDEX` and `DROP INDEX` statements on its own fresh copy, then asks SQLite for the plan of a search for one owner's animals and of a join from the owners of one town to their animals, and looks for your index in each.
nextSteps: Write `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` in front of a query for one owner's animals, and run it.
Which column of `animals` holds the owner? Make an index on it.
Run it again, and try the plan of a join from `owners` to `animals` too.
hints: Read the lesson's part "Reading a plan". In a join from owners to animals, what does SQLite look up in `animals` for each owner?
A column that points at another table is the one a join looks up, so it is the one to index.
The statement has the shape `CREATE INDEX animals_by_owner ON animals (...);`.

docs.title: How the query planner uses indexes

tasks.title: Index one vet's visits by date
tasks.description:
Ifan and Mabel each look at their own visits from a date on: one vet, and every date after a day.

In `queries/3-vet-and-date.sql`, write one `CREATE INDEX` that SQLite uses for both parts of that search, the vet and the date, and read its plan with `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`.

Check runs only your `CREATE INDEX` and `DROP INDEX` statements on its own fresh copy, then asks SQLite for the plan of a search for one vet's visits from a date on, and looks for your index searching on both the vet and the date.
nextSteps: Write `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` in front of the search in the file's comment, and run it.
Make one index on both columns, and read the plan: what is in the brackets after its name?
If only one column is in the brackets, change the order of the columns in your index.
hints: Read the lesson's part "An index on two columns". Which part of the search compares with `=`, and which with `>=`?
An index on two columns is ordered by the first, then by the second within each first. Put the column compared with `=` first, so all of one vet's visits sit together in date order.
The statement has the shape `CREATE INDEX visits_by_vet_and_date ON visits (vet, ...);`.

tasks.title: Remove the index nobody uses
tasks.description:
Every index costs: it takes room, and every `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` on its table has to change it too. `schema.sql` has three indexes, and `practice-queries.sql` holds the queries the practice runs every day.

In `queries/4-unused-index.sql`, read the plan of each query in `practice-queries.sql`, find the index that none of them uses, and remove that one with `DROP INDEX`. Leave the other two.

Check runs only your `CREATE INDEX` and `DROP INDEX` statements on its own fresh copy, and looks at which indexes are left.
nextSteps: Copy each query from `practice-queries.sql` into the file with `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` in front of it, and run it.
Note which index each plan names. Which index of `schema.sql` is never named?
Remove that one, and run the file again: the plans of the other queries should not change.
hints: Read the lesson's part "What an index costs". A plan that says `SCAN` uses no index at all.
An index on a column does not help a `LIKE` pattern that starts with `%`: the start of the value is unknown, so its order is no use.
The statement has the shape `DROP INDEX visits_by_...;`.
